articles.title: New eye-tracking study reveals how followers use gaze to show conscientiousness
articles.summary: New research shows that highly conscientious people strategically direct their gaze at leaders during workplace negotiations. This nonverbal behavior acts as a powerful signal, making them appear more reliable and diligent to their colleagues.

articles.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
articles.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

articles.title: Rare pregnancy infections may triple the risk of autism
articles.summary: A major Swedish study of 3.7 million people has found that rare TORCH infections passed from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to much higher risks of autism and intellectual disability later in life. Children with a congenital TORCH infection were about three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism, more than seven times more likely to have an intellectual disability, and up to 30 times more likely to have severe to profound intellectual disability.

articles.title: Intelligence and personality traits do not predict inattentional blindness
articles.summary: Being smart, focused, or detail-oriented won’t stop you from missing unexpected objects hidden in plain sight. New research suggests that inattentional blindness is a universal quirk of the brain.

articles.title: PsyPost deploys audit program to track retracted and corrected scientific studies in its archive
articles.summary: When science corrects itself, science news should too. PsyPost has launched a custom Python program to daily audit its archive against Retraction Watch and Crossref, ensuring readers are promptly alerted when covered studies are retracted or flagged.

articles.title: Plant-based meat labels make food seem less masculine, study finds
articles.summary: A new study indicates that simply labeling a dish as "plant-based" makes meat-eaters view it as less masculine. This leads to more negative evaluations, especially among individuals who hold hostile sexist beliefs.

articles.title: The Drift Contract: Spectral Updates for Depth-Robust Local Learning
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.26811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local learning trains each layer with its own auxiliary loss and no global backward pass, which makes layer updates structurally parallel. Two problems have kept it marginal: accuracy degrades as depth grows, and hyperparameters are fragile. We apply Muon-style spectral update geometry (momentum orthogonalization with spectral step scaling) to per-layer local updates, an intersection not previously studied. articles.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
articles.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

articles.title: New study reveals that fluctuating—not just intense—brain signals play a hidden role in overeating
articles.summary: A recent study links inconsistent brain reward signals to higher body weight and erratic eating patterns. The research suggests that fluctuating neural responses, rather than consistently strong cravings, may drive overeating and certain eating disorders.
